name: OAuth2 Proxy
summary: A reverse-proxy authentication boundary that turns OAuth2/OIDC provider sessions into authenticated requests and forwards authorized traffic to configured upstreams.

features.name: Reverse-proxy authentication boundary
features.description: The proxy routes authentication endpoints and protected requests through middleware before forwarding requests to configured upstream servers.
benefits: Adds authentication without requiring each upstream application to implement the provider protocol
Provides a single place for request and response header policy
costs: The proxy becomes part of every protected request path
Incorrect trusted-proxy or header configuration can change the security boundary

features.name: Provider adapter and authorization pipeline
features.description: A configured provider adapter performs OAuth2/OIDC login and session validation, while provider-specific claims can be used by authorization checks and forwarded to upstreams.
benefits: Supports multiple provider protocols behind a common proxy contract
Keeps provider-specific token and claim handling behind an adapter
costs: Provider behavior and supported claims are not uniform
Authentication correctness depends on external identity-provider availability and configuration

features.name: Encrypted session storage choices
features.description: The default cookie store keeps encrypted session state client-side, while the Redis store keeps encrypted session data server-side and places a short ticket handle in the cookie.
benefits: Cookie storage can make a deployment stateless
Redis storage reduces per-request cookie size and centralizes session data
costs: Cookie storage has concurrent refresh conflicts and size constraints
Redis storage adds a stateful dependency and expiration coordination

features.name: Composable request middleware chain
features.description: Pre-authentication, session, and header middleware chains are assembled around route handlers for readiness checks, session loading, validation, and upstream handling.
benefits: Makes cross-cutting authentication steps reusable across endpoints
Allows token, cookie, and basic-auth mechanisms to be combined in a route-specific order
costs: Ordering and short-circuit behavior become part of the security contract
Debugging requires tracing behavior across middleware and endpoint handlers

mathematical_views.question: Which transitions take a request from unauthenticated access through provider login, session validation, authorization, and upstream forwarding?
assumptions: A request has an observable route, session state, and authorization result
Provider redirects and callbacks are modeled as external transitions
An upstream response is emitted only after the configured middleware chain completes

mathematical_views.question: How can the same logical authenticated session be represented either directly in a protected cookie or indirectly by an encrypted Redis record and ticket?
assumptions: Both stores implement the same logical session load and save operations
Encryption and signature validation are modeled as representation-preserving boundaries
Backend availability and cookie-size limits are outside semantic equivalence

benefits: Centralized authentication for otherwise unmodified upstreams
costs: Adds a latency and availability dependency before the upstream

benefits: Common request boundary across several identity providers
costs: Provider-specific semantics and external failures remain visible to applications

benefits: Choice between stateless operation and smaller client cookies
costs: The choice exchanges backend dependency for cookie-size and refresh-concurrency constraints
Chain order and short-circuit paths increase operational reasoning burden
